OPS04-BP01 Employ and test safe deployment strategies
Safe deployment practices control how a change reaches customers, so
    that a defect affects the fewest of them before you catch it. When
    you release changes in increments and check health at each step, you
    limit the scope of impact and shorten recovery time.
Desired outcome:
Your delivery pipeline releases production changes in
        incremental stages rather than to all customers at once.
You have automated health checks at each stage that must pass
        before the change proceeds to the next.
Your deployment strategy matches each workload's fault isolation
        boundaries, so a failed change is contained to a single host,
        cell, or Availability Zone.
You select and apply a documented safe deployment strategy for
        every production change.
Common anti-patterns:
Teams deploy a change to all of production at once, so a defect
        reaches every customer at the same time.
An in-place update overwrites the running version, which forces
        a second change to restore the previous version and extends
        recovery time.
Release coordination depends on manual planning across several
        teams, which limits how often teams can ship features.
Deployments proceed without automated health checks, so failures
        surface only after customers report them.
Benefits of establishing this best
    practice:
A defective change affects a fraction of customers instead of
        all of them, because deployment stops before full rollout.
Recovery is faster because the previous version stays available
        and traffic can shift back to it.
Teams deploy more often and with more confidence, because safety
        controls reduce the cost of a failed change.
Emergency releases become rare, because most defects are caught
        in an early stage.
Level of risk exposed if this best practice
    is not established:
Medium
Implementation guidance
A fractional deployment releases the change to a small portion of
      your fleet, verifies it against health signals, then expands in
      controlled increments.
Fractional deployments work best when the increments align with
      your
fault isolation boundaries
— the host, cell, Availability Zone,
      or Region that contains the effect of a failure. AWS structures
      this as waves and stages. A
wave
is a fault
      container, such as a Region, that deploys in parallel with other
      containers. Within a wave, the change moves through
stages
: a one-box stage that takes one host's
      worth of traffic, then progressively larger fractions within one
      Availability Zone. Each stage ends with
bake
      time
to observe health metrics before the next begins.
      Without bake time, you expand before problems surface.
Several strategies implement this pattern, differing in cost,
      speed, and rollback behavior. Rolling deployments replace
      instances in batches and use the least extra capacity, but a
      failure can leave the fleet in a mixed-version state. Immutable
      and blue/green deployments create a parallel set of resources
      running the new version and shift traffic to it. Rollback shifts
      traffic back, at the cost of running two environments during the
      transition. Canary releases send a small share of live traffic to
      the new version, which catches problems that appear only under
      real load. Feature flags separate deployment from release, so you
      can turn a change on or off without another deployment. Most teams
      combine these.
Avoid in-place updates for high-risk changes. When you modify a
      running system in place and the change fails, you have no clean
      previous version to return to. Recovery then means applying
      another change under pressure, which lengthens downtime.
Take extra care with databases and other stateful resources,
      because you cannot discard and replace them the way you replace
      stateless hosts. Blue/green deployments for managed databases
      create a synchronized staging environment you can test before
      promoting it, so you validate schema and configuration changes
      against production-like data before they take traffic. Plan how
      in-flight transactions and replication are handled during the
      switch.
Figures 1 through 3 show the
AWS CodeDeploy
blue/green workflow for Amazon EC2, Amazon ECS,
      and AWS Lambda. AWS CodeDeploy automates in-place and blue/green
      deployments across these compute types and integrates with
      monitoring, so a failed health check can halt or reverse a
      rollout. See
Automating safe, hands-off deployments
and
My CI/CD pipeline is my release captain
for how these stages
      fit together at scale.

Decouple your continuous integration (CI) pipeline from your
      continuous delivery (CD) pipeline. Services such as
Service Catalog
,
Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR)
, and
AWS Serverless Application Repository
host build artifacts that
      CD pipelines consume. Decoupling improves resilience and
      simplifies deploying across Regions: a single CI pipeline
      publishes the artifact to multiple Regions or accounts, and a
      separate instance of the CD pipeline deploys it in each Region,
      for example through an
AWS CloudFormation StackSet
.
With the pipelines decoupled, you can stage and sequence
      deployments to fit release constraints such as change freezes and
      release schedules. A managed service provider (MSP) or
      software-as-a-service (SaaS) provider can then serve clients with
      different acceptance testing and release approvals from a single
      build.
Deployment windows are a separate constraint from fault isolation.
      Some fleets accept changes only during specific hours, such as
      Regions with restricted operating-hour windows, or teams spread
      across time zones with no single window that works for everyone.
      When a narrow window limits how much of your fleet you can update
      in one pass, shorten each deployment's duration so more of the
      fleet completes within the time available. Track how many
      pipelines have no valid window at all, and widen those windows
      deliberately.
Implementation steps
Gate promotion to production with an
            approval workflow:
Trigger the production rollout
            sequence when a change is promoted to production, so the
            safe deployment stages run consistently for every release.
Automate deployments with a managed
            deployment service:
Use
AWS CodeDeploy
to run your chosen strategy. Its
deployment options
include in-place deployments for Amazon EC2
            and on-premises instances, and blue/green deployments for
            Amazon EC2, AWS Lambda, and Amazon ECS. Where useful,
integrate AWS CodeDeploy with other AWS services
.
Apply blue/green deployments to
            stateful resources:
Use managed blue/green
            deployments for databases such as
Amazon Aurora
and
Amazon RDS
, so you validate changes in a synchronized
            staging environment before promotion.
Monitor each deployment
            stage:
Monitor deployments
with Amazon CloudWatch, AWS CloudTrail,
            and Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS)
            notifications, so a stage that breaches its health criteria
            stops the rollout.
Run automated post-deployment
            tests:
After each stage, run functional,
            security, regression, integration, and load tests that
            confirm the change behaves as expected before the next
            increment begins.
Establish deployment troubleshooting
            procedures:
Document how to
troubleshoot deployment issues
and reverse a rollout, so
            responders act from a known procedure rather than
            improvising during an incident.
Automate scheduling within
            constrained deployment windows:
For fleets
            restricted to narrow deployment windows, use
AWS Systems Manager Maintenance Windows
to schedule
            deployment tasks within the time available, and measure the
            fraction of your fleet with no valid window so you can
            prioritize automation that shortens per-deployment duration.
